title: 10 takeaways for the trades from Groundbreak 2026
summary: Procore's all-in-one construction management software platform enables you to finish quality projects—safely, on time, and within budget.
body_markdown:
### **1. The workforce gap makes every worker's time more valuable**


[Procore's report on the future of the specialty contractor](https://www.procore.com/ebooks/future-state-specialty-contractor-strategic-analysis) , cited in the keynote session, found that about 41 percent of the construction workforce is set to retire by 2031, and more than half of workers report extreme burnout.


Even strong recruiting will not close that gap, so the focus shifts to giving your existing workers more time for skilled work. Procore speakers pointed to admin time as the place to find it, citing roughly 18 percent of project time spent looking for information that already exists.


### **2. The cheapest line can cost the most when it is missing**


Tony Leopold, Chief Technology and Strategy Officer at United Rentals, said rental typically makes up[2–3 percent of project value](https://www.procore.com/blog/owned-rented-equipment-one-view) , but equipment that is not where it needs to be creates schedule costs that run much higher.


Seeing owned and rented equipment in one place, with usage data, helps teams catch idle units and plan ahead instead of scrambling.


**Watch the webinar:**[How Procore + United Rentals Bridge the Resource Gap](https://www.procore.com/webinars/how-procore-united-rentals-bridge-the-resource-gap)


### **3. Spreadsheets are a symptom, not a system**


On the materials panel, contractors described receipts that never reached the office, vendors paid without a clear record of what arrived, and material reordered that was already on hand.


Their fix was one system of record that connects orders, receipts, and invoices so the office and the field see the same stock.


**Read more:**[Track your construction materials from purchase to installation](https://www.procore.com/blog/track-your-construction-materials-from-purchase-to-installation)


### **4. Margin leaks in 3 places: Idle crews, unpaid change work, and rework**


Luc D'Abreau, Procore Solution Specialist, said many specialty contractors run on margins of about 1–3 percent. Crews wait on information, change work is not documented fast enough to get paid, and rework comes out of profit.


The proof is usually already in RFIs, submittals, and daily logs. The challenge is finding it quickly.


[Explore Procore AI agents](https://www.procore.com/ai/agents) **for drafting RFIs, reviewing submittals, and more.**


### **5. Know whether a job is making money while you can still steer**


One panelist shared how time, equipment, and production data flowing into the budget let his team see problems the same day instead of a week or two later.


The product keynote described rate tables and production tracking that put hours and earned progress side by side for the same reason.


### **6. Rework is where quality and safety meet**


Panelists said rework sends crews back into hazards they have already faced, often under schedule pressure, and that frustration and complacency never show up in the data.


Their advice: **Document what you saw when you arrived instead of just checking the box, and treat a 100 percent pass rate as a warning sign.**


One quality leader found a pattern of identical easy answers on inspections, rewrote the questions, retrained crews, and saw the pattern drop within about three months.


### **7. Leading indicators beat lagging ones**


An Operational Excellence Manager at an electrical contractor said labor overruns late in a job are a lagging signal that arrives too late.


His team tracks leading behaviors instead: whether three-week look-aheads are done and shared, RFIs and submittals move on time, and approved change orders are reflected in contract value. They manage this through Procore Action Plans and report it in Power BI.


### **8. AI works best when it starts with the records you already keep**


Procore speakers described agents for deep search, RFIs, scheduling analysis, daily logs, and site safety. They said answers cite their sources, the AI sees only what each user can see in Procore, and a person stays in control of what gets approved.


Their practical advice? Start with one small use on one project.


**Go deeper:**[Read the AI implementation guide for construction](https://www.procore.com/ebooks/construction-ai-implementation-guide)


### **9. Standardize before you automate**


One panelist spoke about the limits of automation: It's impossible to automate a broken process. This point was echoed by Kris Lengieza, Field COO at Procore. **Automation on top of a bad process only makes a bad process faster.**


Contractors who wrote down startup expectations item by item, ran a company-wide playbook, or cleaned up their equipment data before loading it into Procore all described doing the standards work first.


### **10. Change sticks when the field helps shape it and leaders own it**


Panelists across sessions gave similar advice. Spend time with crews first so you are not making the field do extra work to fix an office visibility problem. Build champions the field trusts, bring skeptics in early, and expect it to take time.


Leaders have to drive it, and one executive team leads its own deployment committees.
